content:Speaker user says: Given the text: Can we implant and alter memories deliberately? It’s a recurring theme in our pop culture, from Total Recall to Christopher Nolan’s Inception. The preliminary answer to that is a theoretical Yes.
There’s a famous saying from a relatively new branch of psychology called Narrative Psychology: “It’s never too late to have a happy childhood.” This principle lies at the heart of new therapeutic practices that help patients reconstitute and reinterpret traumatic memories into more positive ones. While the details of the memory are not deliberately changed (in most cases, we believe) the meaning of those memories, even the specificity of them, are indeed altered to aid in the patient’s healing process. And in reality, we humans often create revisionist memories, either to block out the bad ones or to create another happier reality.
We know, first of all, that we’re altering our own memories every time we remember them. Technologies such as writing, photography, film/videography, audio recording – of course help us to reinforce the original memory with a greater degree of accuracy. But even when we watch a movie for the second or seventh time, each time the experience is a little different. And each time, we may see something that we didn’t remember from a previous viewing.
But what are the possibilities when it comes to implanting new memories? Can we take a page from narrative psychology and help our audiences remember important parts of their lives differently, in order to bond them with our brands?
The recent campaign called “Go RV’ing” tries to do this. In a very well produced YouTube film, it tells us that when we (presumably grownups) were children, we had the freedom of going outside and riding our bicycles, going camping, exploring the wilderness, and not being glued to our devices or caged in our houses by anxious parents. “Kids want their wildhoods back,” it exhorts us.
As I was watching the film, which I found very evocative, I agreed with the premise. I have many clear memories of exploring the forest behind our apartment building in Chatham, New Jersey, of riding my bike a few miles across town to visit my friends, of bringing home insects and salamanders to my rather horrified mother after forays into the woods. Yes, I thought, there must be a lot of people like me, who remember those experiences and compare them to the caged and wired world that our children experience today.
At the same time, I had to wonder: In some cases, is this campaign ‘incepting’ these memories in the audience? Is it intensifying those memories into a kind of Garden of Eden, where we’re led to believe our children have been expelled from a kind of paradise? Perhaps so. And if that’s the case, then this campaign is very cleverly using the creative quality of memory to instill longing and emotion. I fully they’re going to sell RV’s to lots of Canadian families.

content:Speaker assistant says: There are various new therapeutic practices that aim to help patients reconstitute and reinterpret traumatic memories into more positive ones. Narrative psychology is one such approach that focuses on the storytelling aspect of memory. This involves helping patients to reconceptualize their past experiences by creating a new narrative about their lives. Other techniques include cognitive restructuring, exposure therapy, and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), which involves recalling traumatic memories while engaging in bilateral sensory input, such as eye movements or tapping.

The goal of these therapies is to help patients develop new, more positive associations with their traumatic memories and reduce the emotional distress and anxiety that may be associated with them. While the details of the memory are not deliberately changed, the meaning and interpretation of the memory can be altered to promote healing and psychological well-being. These techniques are often used to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other trauma-related disorders. context:This text discusses new therapies designed to reshape traumatic memories into more positive experiences, utilizing techniques like narrative reconstruction and cognitive restructuring to alleviate emotional distress and promote psychological well-being, particularly in the context of PTSD and related disorders. keywords: traumatic memories, therapeutic practices, narrative psychology, PTSD tags: Mental Health, Therapy, Trauma, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Catfish Parlour. Multiple locations. Catfishparlour.com. Fried oysters, fried okra, fried shrimp, and, yes, fried catfish at the three Austin-area locations of this downhome spot.
Cherry Creek Catfish Company. 5712 Manchaca Road. 512-440-8810, cherrycreekcatfish.com. The name says it all at this casual South Austin restaurant that has been serving Southern-fried comfort for more than 20 years.
Clark’s. 1200 W. Sixth St. 512-297-2525, clarksoysterbar.com. This jewel-box oyster bar looks like it was snatched up from the Hamptons, dusted of sand and placed in West Austin. If you’re lucky, you can snag one of the few outdoor tables lining the front windows.
Deckhand Oyster Bar. 500 Parker Drive. 512-368-3379, deckhandoysterbar.com. Flavor profiles range from Southwestern to Southeast Asian at this oyster palace in North Austin.
Eddie V’s. 301 E. Fifth St. 512-472-1860; 9400B Arboretum Blvd. 512-342-2642; eddievs.com. The Austin-born franchise has a classic steakhouse vibe and popular all-night happy hours Sunday and Monday.
Evangeline Café. 8106 Brodie Lane. 512-282-2586, EvangelineCafe.com. Take a trip to the bayou at this Cajun restaurant in South Austin for gumbo, po’ boys and music by the likes of Charles Thibodeaux and the Austin Cajun Aces.
Finn & Porter. 500 E. Fourth St. 512-493-4900, finnandporteraustin.com. The fine dining restaurant at the Hilton serves a wide array of seafood, from scallops and octopus to branzino and sea bass.
Freda’s Seafood Grille. 10903 Pecan Park Blvd. 512-506-8700, fredasseafoodgrille.com. Mango tilapia, shrimp and grits, Chilean sea bass … this locally owned restaurant near Lakeline Mall has a seafood menu that runs the gamut.
Garbo’s. 14735 Bratton Lane. 512-350-9814, garboslobsteratx.com. The restaurant in Wells Branch expands its food truck menu to include fish spreads, grilled fish, a solid burger and more, in addition to the excellent lobster rolls.
Liberty Kitchen. 507 Pressler St. 512-840-1330, libertykitchenatx.com. Houston-based Liberty Kitchen’s wide-ranging menu includes oysters from around the country, caviar tastings, lobster rolls and much more.
Mongers Market and Kitchen. 2401 E. Cesar Chavez St. 512-215-8972, mongersaustin.com. Partners Roberto San Miguel and chef Shane Stark use their Gulf Coast connections to source seafood for dishes like Gulf red snapper and barbecue Gulf shrimp.
Pappadeaux. 6319 Interstate 35 N. 512-452-9363, pappadeaux.com. The Pappas family of Houston bring flavors of the Big Easy to several of their seafood platters.
Perla’s. 1400 S. Congress Ave. 512-291-7300, perlasaustin.com. Expansive patio offers great people-watching while eating seafood on landlocked South Congress Avenue.
Searsucker. 415 Colorado St. 512-394-8000, searsucker.com/austin. Celebrity chef Brian Malarkey marries coastal cuisine with Texas flavors at this massive restaurant in the Warehouse District.
Quality Seafood Market. 5621 Airport Blvd. 512-452-3820, qualityseafood.wordpress.com. One of Austin’s most beloved homes of seafood, Quality Seafood features a huge oyster bar in the middle of the restaurant serving Gulf oysters and East coast varieties on the half-shell — and really cold beer.
Shoal Creek Saloon. 909 N. Lamar Blvd. 512-474-0805, shoalcreeksaloon.com. Crawfish etouffee nods to this restaurant’s love for Louisiana, and there’s more fried seafood than you can shake a shrimp at.
Truluck’s. 400 Colorado St. 512-482-9000; 10225 Research Blvd. 512-794-8300; trulucks.com. content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly, here are some tips on how to properly attach findings to your jewelry:

1. Use the right size: Make sure you use the right size of findings for your project. If they are too small, they won't be secure, and if they are too big, they will look awkward.

2. Secure your findings properly: Use pliers to crimp jump rings or use a secure knot to tie your cords. Whatever method you choose, make sure that your findings are securely attached and won't come loose.

3. Check for sharp edges: After attaching jump rings or clasps, check for any sharp or rough edges. Use pliers to smooth them out, as they can snag on clothing or scratch your skin.

4. Add a drop of glue: If you want added security, add a drop of jewelry glue to your jump rings or clasps before attaching them. This will prevent them from shaking loose over time.

5. Create a seamless finish: Once you've attached the findings, make sure everything looks seamless. The jump rings should be closed tightly, and the clasps should line up with your jewelry properly and not be twisted.

6. Test fit: Before finishing your piece, try it on and test it to make sure it fits well and is comfortable to wear.

By following these tips, you can successfully attach your findings to your jewelry pieces and create beautiful and durable pieces. context:This guide provides practical instructions for securely attaching findings to jewelry, emphasizing proper sizing, secure fastening techniques, and the importance of a seamless finish to ensure durability and comfort. keywords: findings, jewelry, crimping, securing, adhesion tags: Jewelry Making, Crafting, Security, Design

content:Speaker assistant says: Absolutely, here are some tips on choosing the right wire for your jewelry:

1. Consider the intended purpose of your jewelry: The type of wire you choose for your jewelry will depend on what you are creating. For example, thicker wire may be better suited for making bracelets or cuffs for added structure and support, while thinner wire may work better for wire-wrapped stones or beaded necklaces.

2. Choose the right material: Wires can be made from a variety of materials such as gold, silver, copper, brass, and stainless steel. Each material has its strengths and weaknesses, so think about what material will work best for your project and your budget.

3. Consider the wire gauge: The wire gauge determines the thickness of the wire. The higher the gauge number, the thinner the wire will be. For most jewelry projects, you will want to work with a wire that is between 18 and 22 gauge.

4. Look at flexibility: The flexibility of the wire will also impact how you use it. Soft wire is malleable and easy to bend, while hard wire is stiffer and more challenging to bend but holds its shape well.

5. Choose the finish: The finish of the wire can make a big difference in the appearance of your jewelry. Some options include a shiny or matte finish, or colored wire. Think about what will work best with the beads and stones you have chosen.

By keeping these factors in mind when choosing wire for your jewelry, you can create beautiful and lasting pieces. context:This passage provides guidance on selecting appropriate wire for jewelry creation, emphasizing the importance of purpose, material choice, gauge, flexibility, and finish to achieve desired results. keywords: wire, jewelry, materials, gauge tags: jewelry making, materials, design

- Beading thread
- Beading needle
- Clasp
- Crimp beads
- Crimping tool

Step 1: Choose your color scheme and gather your materials. You can use a combination of colors or stick to a monochromatic look.

Step 2: Cut a length of beading thread that is twice the length of your desired bracelet size. Thread a beading needle onto one end of the thread, and tie a knot at the other end.

Step 3: Begin by threading a crimp bead onto the thread and passing the thread through one end of the clasp. Loop the thread back through the crimp bead, and use the crimping tool to secure the clasp in place.

Step 4: Begin adding seed beads and accent beads in your desired pattern. You can choose to create a repeating pattern or randomly add beads. Make sure to leave enough room at the end of the thread to attach the other half of the clasp.

Step 5: Once you have reached your desired length, add another crimp bead and pass the thread through the other end of the clasp. Loop the thread back through the crimp bead, and use the crimping tool to secure the clasp in place.

Step 6: Trim any excess thread, and your bracelet is ready to wear!

- Complementary: choose two opposite colors on the color wheel, such as blue and orange, for a bold contrast
- Analogous: choose three colors that are beside each other on the color wheel, such as blue-green and green, for a cohesive look

materials needed:

2. Design template: you can either draw a design freehand or print an image to use as a guide.

3. Metal shears: used for cutting the sheet metal to the required size.

4. Deburring tool: used to smooth the rough edges of the sheet metal.

5. Hammer: used for shaping the metal.

6. Punches & chisels: used for making holes and fine details.

7. Sandpaper: used for smoothing the metal surface.

8. Paint or varnish: used to give the piece a finishing touch.

steps:

1. First, prepare a design template or print out an image to use as a guide.

2. Cut the sheet metal to the desired size with metal shears.

3. Use the deburring tool to smoothen rough edges and clean the metal surface.

4. Tape the template or image on the sheet metal and trace the design with a fine chisel.

5. Use the punch and chisel tools to make holes and fine details. You can also use a hammer to shape and add texture.

6. Sand the metal surface with fine grit sandpaper until all the rough edges are removed.

7. Clean the metal surface with a damp cloth and let it dry completely.

8. Add a coat of paint or varnish to give the piece a finishing touch.

Additionally, adding a coat of paint or varnish can give the piece a unique touch and protect it from corrosion.
